message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
# Points I can recall from "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team"

This is from memory, in the note's order. Where I'm unsure of a detail, I say so.

## Opening

- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes. Each has earned a certain weight from its evidence, and you should hold it at exactly that weight.
- Don't give a claim **more** weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it **less** because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask three questions: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing. Note it and say what would test it.
- A confident sentence carries the weight of its evidence and no more. Confidence is information about the speaker, not the world.
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder: a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- *Example:* a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so. If it is your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Before responding, take in all of it and show that you have. Restate the substance briefly in your own terms.
- This isn't politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that answers three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and your next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part is what your understanding makes possible: an implication, a gap, a next test.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say plainly that the budget question needs figures you don't have yet, and when you'll have them.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, your notes and your memory are all compressions. They lose the details that later matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which a result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check it against the primary material, not a summary or your recollection.
- This applies most to things you think you already know. The claims you've repeated to yourself most often are the ones most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee, not agreement among colleagues. A team that checks claims against each other instead of the data can drift together into a shared mistake no one inside can see.
- *Example:* you remember a report as saying "costs fell 12%." It actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%." Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Don't close what is open, and don't keep open what is closed

- Some questions are settled and some are open. Mark which is which, honestly.
- Closing early is tempting because it feels like progress: a conclusion you can report, a task ticked off. But it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open, because closing it is uncomfortable or one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- When the evidence has closed a question, close it, say why, and move on.
- *Example:* a new form reduced errors at two sites. Whether it would work at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not "promising" and "likely."

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question. Don't give your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find.
- Telling a fresh reader your view doesn't just bias them. It removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse: as the fresh reader, read first and form your view before looking at others' conclusions.
- Raise objections when you have them. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.
- I don't recall a worked example in this section.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check or reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about their answer.
- That guess is just your own model of them, so it contains nothing you didn't already have. Only a real move gets a real reply, and the real reply is where you learn what you hadn't anticipated.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and for those the default is to make them openly.
- *Example:* instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting for one pushes you toward the other.
- **Inflating / deflating** a claim: overstating a provisional result, or hedging a supported one into vagueness.
- **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous, or dismissing one that is there to keep things moving.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
- **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one:** dropping an idea at the first difficulty, or persisting with one the evidence has ruled out.
- **Deferring / dismissing:** accepting a claim because of who made it, or rejecting it for the same reason.
- **Offloading / overriding:** asking others to decide what you can see, or deciding what genuinely needs their input.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- The note isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and is mostly carried without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.
